study.title: Ninety credits in the age of AI: who holds American construction degrees at 120, what a cut would give and take, and how a program could reach 90
study.abstract: Since September 2024 U.S. institutional accreditors have opened routes to bachelor’s degrees below 120 credits, and a federal rule of October 2026 tells them not to bar such degrees when outcomes are comparable. Programs lag: 119 were announced by May 2026, and by November a public university had one approved in only 10 states, none in construction. This study asks who holds a construction management degree at 120 credits, what a cut would give and take, and how a program could reach 90. In veto player terms, a 90-credit degree must satisfy at once the state, the institution, both of its accreditors and the program. An integer program found the smallest degree that satisfies every holder for each of 81 accredited or applicant programs. No holder alone claims more than 75 of the 90 credits, yet cut to the floors of the American Council for Construction Education (ACCE), only 39 programs fit 90: 25 of 28 where the state’s general education count is 30 hours or fewer, none of 21 where it is 37 to 43. Held to ACCE’s outcomes instead of its hours, all 81 fit; with 12 major hours counted as general education, 75; keeping today’s courses, 5. The median student would gain $91,047, which pay 3.2% lower over a career would cancel, and an institution loses money unless 25% of a 90-credit program’s students are new to it. The study shows that the 120 is held by the sum of the holders’ rules, not by any one of them: no holder can shorten the degree alone, and opening routes, as the accreditors and the federal rule have done, does not by itself reach an accredited field. Three implications follow. First, outside the states that count 30 hours or fewer, a 90-credit construction degree needs ACCE to accept its outcomes in fewer hours, or states and accreditors to let major courses count as general education, taught rather than relabeled. Second, a program must then decide which hours to keep, not how many to cut, and keep the internship, the technical foundations and the judgment that checks AI output. Third, because the student’s gain would vanish with a small pay penalty and the institution gains only from new students, the degree should be offered first to transfer students and working adults.
study.keywords: reduced-credit degree; accreditation; general education; veto players; construction management; artificial intelligence
rqs: RQ1. Where does the 90-credit construction degree stand in 2026, and who holds U.S. construction management programs at 120 credits?
RQ2. What would a 90-credit degree give and take from students, institutions, employers and the profession, and where does the gain turn into a loss?
RQ3. By which routes could a construction management program reach 90 credits within ACCE’s and ABET’s terms, under which state rules, and what would each route remove?
RQ4. What should programs, states and accreditors do, in what order and for which students, now that AI changes which skills a degree must protect?
hypotheses: H1. No holder alone requires 120 credits, or even 90: each holder’s own demand fits within a 90-credit degree.

H2. The holders’ demands together exceed 90 credits for many programs, and whether they do depends on the general education count a state or accreditor asks, with a threshold the rules predict: ACCE’s 62 professional hours plus the count, less the 3 hours of economics that count toward both, fit 90 only up to a count of 31.

H3. The overlap, a decision that belongs to states, systems and institutional accreditors rather than to programs, brings into the winset most of the programs that a cut to the accreditor’s floor leaves outside it.
H4. ACCE’s hour floors, not its outcomes, bind the professional part of the degree; ANSAC, which counts no hours, binds only through the topics and outcomes it names.
H5. A program that keeps its present courses cannot reach 90 credits in almost any state: the program is itself a veto player.
theory: Tsebelis (2002) calls an actor whose agreement is required to change the status quo a veto player. The outcomes that can defeat the status quo form its winset; where every veto player must agree, the winset holds only what all of them prefer to the status quo, so it cannot grow as veto players are added or as their positions move apart, and policy stability rises, or at least does not fall, with their number and their distance (Tsebelis, 2002, pp. 19 to 21). The theory was built for legislatures and coalitions, but its logic is general: a status quo that no one chose can persist because every alternative is refused by someone.

Degree length fits the logic closely. A 90-credit construction degree needs the agreement of five holders: the state or system that sets a general education count for public universities, the institutional accreditor that sets one for the institution, the institution that keeps its own core, the programmatic accreditor that sets professional hours and outcomes, and the program that decides which of its courses to keep (Table 2). None of them asks for 120 credits. Each asks for a part, and the parts can exceed 90 when they are added. In the language of the theory, the 120 is stable if the winset of the four-year degree at 90 credits is empty: if no 90-credit curriculum satisfies every holder, no holder can move the degree alone, and a holder that relaxes its rule changes nothing until the others have relaxed theirs.

The second theory concerns what a curriculum must keep. Under constructive alignment, the intended outcomes are used to align teaching methods and assessment (Biggs, 1996). The study takes the corollary that an outcome a curriculum neither teaches nor assesses is not met, so a shorter degree must keep a course for each outcome. A 90-credit design that satisfied ACCE’s hours but kept no course for one of its outcomes would not meet ACCE’s terms, and neither would one that kept a course for every outcome but not the hours. The study therefore treats an outcome as a constraint on the courses a design keeps, not only on its hours. Five hypotheses follow from the two theories and the rules.
study.theory_heading: Theory: holders with a veto, and outcomes met through courses

ai_evidence.text: Endoscopists’ adenoma detection rate in colonoscopies without AI fell from 28.4% to 22.4% after routine exposure to AI (1,443 patients)
Outside the frontier of what AI does well, knowledge workers using it were correct about 19 percentage points less often; inside it they completed 12.2% more tasks
Knowledge workers with more confidence in AI reported less critical thinking (319 workers)
Automation bias affects experts as well as novices, and training does not remove it
Operators who only monitor automation lose the skill to take over when it fails

Three risks for learners: deskilling, the loss of previously acquired skills; mis-skilling, the reinforcement of incorrect behavior due to AI errors or bias; never-skilling, the failure to develop essential competencies
Students using ChatGPT improved essay scores without more knowledge gain or transfer
AI raised productivity by 15% on average and by 30% for less skilled and less experienced workers
Intelligent tutoring systems raise test performance by a median .66 standard deviations across 50 evaluations
A tutor designed to give one step at a time rather than the full solution doubled learning gains in less time in a randomized crossover trial (median 49 minutes against a 60-minute class)
Open access to GPT-4 raised practice grades by 48% but lowered grades on an exam taken without AI by 17%; a tutor that gave teacher-designed hints removed that loss
ChatGPT produced construction schedules that were coherent but contained wrong tasks
Model-based estimating still leaves the estimator substantial work
Junior employment fell about 9% at firms adopting generative AI, through fewer hires (working paper)
